notes:
Here are my verse-by-verse notes on Genesis 28, drawn from the sources I was able to access.

---

## Genesis 28 — Verse-by-Verse Notes

### v. 1 — “So Isaac called for Jacob and blessed him. ‘Do not take a wife from the Canaanite women,’ he commanded.”

- **Isaac's willing blessing.** By now Isaac had resigned himself to God's will — that the older would serve the younger (Gen 25:23). He blesses Jacob "with hearty cheerfulness" and confirms him as the possessor of the birthright, with no attempt to substitute Esau. (Ellicott) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/28.htm
- **The marriage charge.** Rebekah's concern for Jacob's safety was real, but the marriage question was no mere pretext. Now that Jacob was acknowledged as firstborn, arranging a proper marriage was a duty. (Ellicott) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/28.htm
- **Contrast with Esau.** It was essential Jacob not marry a Canaanite woman as Esau had done. As the heir of the birthright and the Messianic line, he must seek a wife among his uncle Laban's daughters. (Guzik, Enduring Word) https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-28/

### v. 2 — “Go at once to Paddan-aram, to the house of your mother’s father Bethuel, and take a wife from among the daughters of Laban, your mother’s brother.”

- **Isaac's intimate knowledge.** Isaac shows a much closer acquaintance with the family at Haran than Abraham had possessed. This greater knowledge is why Isaac sent Jacob in person rather than a deputy (as Abraham had done). (Ellicott) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/28.htm
- **Bethuel.** Though we gather from v.5 that Bethuel was now dead, he was a person of more importance than rabbinic tradition supposes. (Ellicott) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/28.htm

### v. 3 — “May God Almighty bless you and make you fruitful and multiply you, so that you may become a company of peoples.”

- **El Shaddai.** Isaac deliberately uses the name "God Almighty" (Heb. *El Shaddai*), the same title God bore in the covenant with Abraham at Genesis 17:1, of which circumcision was the seal. This confirms Jacob in the Abrahamic promises. (Ellicott) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/28.htm ; (Guzik) https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-28/
- **"A company/assembly of peoples."** The Hebrew word (*qahal*) is not the same as in Genesis 17:4 but one signifying an assembly — especially one summoned for religious purposes. Like the Greek *ecclesia* (church), it comes from a root meaning "to convoke." It became the regular term for "the congregation of Israel" (Lev 16:17) and implies the nations descended from Jacob would have a religious significance. (Ellicott) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/28.htm

### v. 4 — “And may He give the blessing of Abraham to you and your descendants, so that you may possess the land where you dwell as a foreigner, the land God gave to Abraham.”

- **The Abrahamic covenant.** After a general blessing of prosperity, Isaac now confers the specific "blessing of Abraham" — the covenant promises of land, descendants, and blessing to all nations (Gen 12:1-3; 15:8; 17:7-8). This was the birthright Esau despised. (Guzik) https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-28/
- **Triumph of sovereignty.** All four parties in the blessing drama of Genesis 27 had acted unspiritually; yet God brought good out of it. Jacob seemed as unworthy as Esau, but God's sovereign election prevailed. (Guzik) https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-28/

### v. 5 — “So Isaac sent Jacob to Paddan-aram, to Laban son of Bethuel the Aramean, the brother of Rebekah, who was the mother of Jacob and Esau.”

- **Oriental style.** The insertion of already-known family details ("the mother of Jacob and Esau") is typical of Hebrew narrative which carefully impresses family relationships on the reader. (Ellicott) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/28.htm
- **Jacob named first.** Now that Jacob has been confirmed in the birthright by both father and mother, his name is placed before Esau's. (Ellicott) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/28.htm
- **Long separation.** Jacob would not see Isaac again for over 20 years. (Guzik) https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-28/

### v. 6 — “Now Esau learned that Isaac had blessed Jacob and sent him to Paddan-aram to take a wife there, commanding him, ‘Do not marry a Canaanite woman,’”

- **Esau's grief.** The solemn transfer of the birthright and Isaac's complete assent to it must have caused Esau real grief. He now realised his own illegitimate Canaanite marriages had contributed to this outcome. (Ellicott) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/28.htm

### v. 7 — “and that Jacob had obeyed his father and mother and gone to Paddan-aram.”

- **Jacob's obedience noted.** The text highlights Jacob's obedience to both father and mother, contrasting with Esau's earlier disregard for parental wishes in marriage. (Guzik) https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-28/

### v. 8 — “And seeing that his father Isaac disapproved of the Canaanite women,”

- **Esau's belated awakening.** Esau now sees that the Canaanite women did not please Isaac. He determines to act, but his remedy is superficial. (Guzik) https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-28/

### v. 9 — “Esau went to Ishmael and married Mahalath, the sister of Nebaioth and daughter of Abraham’s son Ishmael, in addition to the wives he already had.”

- **A well-meaning but misguided act.** Esau avoids Canaanite women but marries into Ishmael's line — a family already separated from the covenant promise by God's own appointment. This shows he still had no grasp of the religious interests of the chosen family. (Keil & Delitzsch, cited in Constable) https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/genesis-28.html
- **Mahalath / Basemath.** She is called Basemath in Genesis 36:3. She is described as "sister of Nebaioth" to show she was the daughter of Ishmael's primary wife, not a concubine, sharing in that precedence. (Ellicott) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/28.htm
- **Polygamy.** Esau "added" this wife to those he already had, further complicating his household. Polygamy was suffered in that era but never had God's blessing upon it. (Pulpit Homiletics) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/genesis/28.htm

### v. 10 — “Meanwhile Jacob left Beersheba and set out for Haran.”

- **The history turns to Jacob.** Though the section is called the *Tôldôth* (generations) of Isaac, from this point forward Jacob's fortunes occupy the narrator. Isaac still had 63 years to live. All prior events had been preparation; now Jacob is confirmed as covenant heir. (Ellicott) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/28.htm

### v. 11 — “On reaching a certain place, he spent the night there because the sun had set. And taking one of the stones from that place, he put it under his head and lay down to sleep.”

- **"The place."** The Hebrew has the definite article — "the place" — suggesting it was divinely appointed for the revelation, though Jacob "lighted upon" it by what seemed chance. (Ellicott) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/28.htm
- **Location.** The site lay about 12 miles north of Jerusalem in the mountains of Ephraim. Jacob had already been on the road at least four days. (Ellicott) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/28.htm
- **Solitude and vulnerability.** Jacob slept on open ground, far from any city, alone and vulnerable — yet this is precisely where God met him. (Ligonier) https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/jacobs-ladder
- **The stones.** Jewish commentators identified this place with Mount Moriah, saying the stone was one from the altar where Isaac had been bound. These explanations are allegorical rather than strictly expository. (Ellicott) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/28.htm
- **Bleak setting.** The site was a "bleak moorland" covered with large sheets of bare rock, "like gravestones." (Precept Austin, citing Stanley's *Sinai and Palestine*) https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis_devotional_commentary

### v. 12 — “And Jacob had a dream about a ladder that rested on the earth with its top reaching up to heaven, and God’s angels were going up and down the ladder.”

- **A stairway, not a household ladder.** The Hebrew *sullam* (a rare word, occurring only here) most likely denotes a staircase or stepped ramp. Many commentators link it to the staircases of ancient ziggurats (temple-towers). (Constable) https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/genesis-28.html ; (Ligonier) https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/jacobs-ladder
- **Contrast with Babel.** At Babel (Gen 11), arrogant sinners tried to climb up into heaven. Here, God in grace takes the first step down toward His chosen man. (Ligonier) https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/jacobs-ladder
- **The angels ascending and descending.** They portray "the real and uninterrupted fellowship between God in heaven and His people upon earth" — carrying up human needs and bringing down divine help. (Keil & Delitzsch, cited in Constable) https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/genesis-28.html
- **Access to heaven.** Jacob now knew that God was closer than he had ever imagined and that there was real, living interaction between heaven and earth. (Guzik) https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-28/
- **Christological meaning.** Jesus explicitly claims to be this ladder in John 1:51: "You shall see heaven open, and the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of Man." He is the way; He does not merely show a way but *is* the way (John 14:6). (Guzik) https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-28/
- **Calvin's view.** John Calvin wrote that Christ "is the medium through which the fullness of all celestial blessings flows down to us, and through which we, in turn, ascend to God." (Ligonier, citing Calvin) https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/jacobs-ladder
- **Spurgeon's emphasis.** "The God of Bethel is a God who does concern himself with the things of earth, not a God who shuts himself up in heaven, but God who hath a ladder fixed between heaven and earth." (Spurgeon, cited in Guzik) https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-28/
- **God sought Jacob.** Nothing indicates Jacob was looking for the Lord; God found him — as He finds all His people (Ps 139; Luke 15; Rom 8:29-30). (Ligonier) https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/jacobs-ladder

### v. 13 — “And there at the top the LORD was standing and saying, ‘I am the LORD, the God of your father Abraham and the God of Isaac. I will give you and your descendants the land on which you now lie.’”

- **Personal encounter.** Jacob had heard of the God of Abraham and Isaac, but now this same God met Jacob personally. This was life-changing. (Guzik) https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-28/
- **The Lord "stationed" above.** The Hebrew verb (*nitsab*) signifies that the Deity holds His permanent station there — He was not there accidentally. (Ellicott) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/28.htm
- **Confirmation of the covenant.** God repeats the land-promise given to Abraham (Gen 12:7; 13:14-16) and Isaac (Gen 26:2-5). Previously Isaac had told Jacob the covenant was his (vv.3-4); now God Himself confirms it. (Guzik) https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-28/
- **Grace at a crucial moment.** Jacob is homeless and his life is endangered. God's visit assures him that Isaac's words were not spoken in vain. (Ligonier) https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/jacobs-ladder

### v. 14 — “Your descendants will be like the dust of the earth, and you will spread out to the west and east and north and south. All the families of the earth will be blessed through you and your offspring.”

- **The threefold promise.** God promises Jacob (a) a land, (b) descendants as innumerable as dust, and (c) that all families of the earth will be blessed through him and his seed. This is the full Abrahamic covenant. (Guzik) https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-28/
- **Universal scope.** The promise that Jacob's offspring will spread to all four compass points is "an early indication that Jacob's family (all those with faith in the Messiah, Gal 3:29) will inherit the earth (Matt 5:5)." (Ligonier) https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/jacobs-ladder
- **Messianic seed.** The "offspring" (*seed*) through whom all families will be blessed is ultimately Christ (Gal 3:16). (Guzik) https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-28/

### v. 15 — “Look, I am with you, and I will watch over you wherever you go, and I will bring you back to this land. For I will not leave you until I have done what I have promised you.”

- **The promise of presence.** The land and descendants promises would be worthless if Jacob did not survive to return and father those descendants. God therefore promises personal protection and presence. (Guzik) https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-28/
- **"I am with you."** Jacob was the second person in the Bible to hear this assurance (Isaac was first: Gen 26:3, 24). God later repeated it to Moses, Joshua, Gideon, and to all Christians (Matt 28:20; Heb 13:5). (Constable) https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/genesis-28.html
- **Spurgeon on presence.** "That God should give to Jacob bread to eat and raiment to put on was much, but it is nothing compared with 'I am with thee.' … This includes countless blessings, but it is in itself a great deal more than all the blessings we can conceive of." (Spurgeon, cited in Guzik) https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-28/
- **Philippians 1:6 echoed.** "I will not leave you until I have done what I have spoken" anticipates the New Testament confidence that "He who has begun a good work in you will complete it" (Phil 1:6). (Guzik) https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-28/
- **Matthew Henry.** "Whom God loves he never leaves." (cited in Ligonier) https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/jacobs-ladder
- **Reformed emphasis.** God's promise is entirely God-centred and unconditional: "I am," "I will give," "I am with you," "I will not leave you." This contrasts sharply with Jacob's conditional vow in vv.20-22. (Guzik) https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-28/

### v. 16 — “When Jacob woke up, he thought, ‘Surely the LORD is in this place, and I was unaware of it.’”

- **Surprise at God's presence.** Jacob was not ignorant of God's omnipresence; what astonished him was that Jehovah would reveal Himself far from the established shrines where He was worshipped (e.g., Beersheba). He felt far from all religious associations of his youth. (Ellicott) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/28.htm
- **A lesson in God's omnipresence.** One great purpose of the dream was to show Jacob that Jehovah watches over the whole earth and that messengers come and go from Him everywhere. (Ellicott) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/28.htm
- **Jacob's limited understanding.** If Jacob thought God was in *this* place but not others, he was mistaken. David later understood this: "Where can I flee from Your presence?" (Ps 139:7). (Guzik) https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-28/

### v. 17 — “And he was afraid and said, ‘How awesome is this place! This is none other than the house of God; this is the gate of heaven!’”

- **Holy fear.** The word "afraid" / "dreadful" describes "a mixture of terror and adoration, a worshipful fear" (cf. Ex 19:16). (Ross, cited in Constable) https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/genesis-28.html
- **"The house of God"** — *Bethel.* This is where God dwells. (Constable) https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/genesis-28.html
- **"The gate of heaven."** The place where Jacob, in his dream, entered heaven — the appointed entrance for prayer now, and for admission to the glorified life hereafter. (Ellicott) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/28.htm ; (Constable) https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/genesis-28.html

### v. 18 — “Early the next morning, Jacob took the stone that he had placed under his head, and he set it up as a pillar. He poured oil on top of it.”

- **A memorial pillar.** Jacob's purpose was to mark the spot for future identification and worship. Unlike his forefathers, he did not build an altar — he set up a standing stone (*massebah*). (Constable) https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/genesis-28.html ; (Ellicott) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/28.htm
- **Oil as consecration.** Pouring oil on the stone was an act of dedication to holy use — oil being the symbol of consecration throughout Scripture. (Ellicott) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/28.htm ; (Constable) https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/genesis-28.html

### v. 19 — “and he called that place Bethel, though previously the city had been named Luz.”

- **Bethel vs. Luz.** In Joshua 16:1-2, Luz and Bethel are distinct though nearby places. Jacob did not enter the Canaanite city but slept in the open. At the time of Joshua's conquest, when Ephraim seized Luz, the name Bethel was transferred to the city. (Ellicott) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/28.htm
- **Bethel's future significance.** Bethel would become second only to Jerusalem in the number of Old Testament mentions. Tragically, it later became a high place of idolatrous sacrifice (1 Kings 13:32; Hosea 10:15; Amos 4:4). (Guzik) https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-28/
- God later referred to Himself as "the God of Bethel" (Gen 31:13). (Guzik) https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-28/

### v. 20 — “Then Jacob made a vow, saying, ‘If God will be with me and watch over me on this journey, and if He will provide me with food to eat and clothes to wear,’”

- **The traditional reading: a conditional bargain.** David Guzik (Pentecostal/Charismatic) reads this as Jacob's spiritual immaturity: God gave him an unconditional promise, yet Jacob responds with "If… then…" bargaining. God's mere word was not enough — Jacob had to see fulfilment first. (Guzik) https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-28/
- **An alternative reading.** Some scholars note the Hebrew can be translated "Since God will be with me…" rather than "If…" This would make Jacob's vow an acceptance of the covenant terms, not a bargain. Constable notes this was "probably not as crass a bargain as it appears," though Jacob's life does show he was "keen on negotiating deals." (Constable) https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/genesis-28.html
- **Ellicott's view.** Ellicott argues the common translation "then shall the Lord be my God" is a false rendering. Jacob's vow "implies no doubt on his part, but is his acceptance of the terms of the covenant." He paraphrases: if God does these things (as promised), then "this stone shall be Beth-Elohim" and Jacob will tithe. The "if" is not doubt but a recapitulation of mercies promised. (Ellicott) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/28.htm
- **Jacob's man-centred terms.** Guzik points out the contrast: God's promise (vv.13-15) is all "I am… I will… I am with you…" Jacob's vow is all "If God will be with me… keep me… give me bread… clothing…" One is God-centred; the other terribly man-centred. (Guzik) https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-28/

### v. 21 — “so that I may return safely to my father's house, then the LORD will be my God.”

- **Jacob "tests" God.** Unlike Abraham, whom God tested, Jacob tested God. God told Abraham to leave before blessing; Jacob imposed conditions before vowing to bless God. "He was willing to accept God's promises, but he did not commit himself to God until God proved faithful to him personally." (Constable, citing Walton) https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/genesis-28.html
- **God's gracious accommodation.** God blessed Jacob because of divine election and the faith of Abraham and Isaac, more than because of Jacob's faith at this stage. God accommodates weak faith, but this does not commend bargaining with God. (Constable) https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/genesis-28.html
- **Guzik's pastoral application.** It would have been better if Jacob had prayed: "Because You promised to be with me and to keep me… I will be completely Yours, God." Believers should trust God's promises without demanding to see fulfilment first. (Guzik) https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-28/

### v. 22 — “And this stone I have set up as a pillar will be God's house, and of all that You give me I will surely give You a tenth.”

- **"God's house."** Jacob apparently meant by *Beth-Elohim* a place where prayer and offerings would be acceptable because God had manifested Himself there. His vow signified that if he returned safely, he would consecrate the spot to Jehovah's service. (Ellicott) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/28.htm
- **The tithe.** This is an early reference to tithing (cf. Gen 14:20, Abraham's tithe to Melchizedek). Jacob promises a tenth of all God gives him. (Constable) https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/genesis-28.html
- **Pillar vs. altar.** Jacob vowed to convert his memorial pillar into a place of worship ("God's house") if God proved faithful — the only recorded time a patriarch proposed a vow with God (cf. Gen 31:13). (Constable) https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/genesis-28.html
- **Jacob's growing faith.** The vow, despite its apparent conditionality, represents a distinct advance in Jacob's religious life. "The hope of blessing became the covenant of engagement, service, worship, sacrifice." (Pulpit Homiletics) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/genesis/28.htm
- **God's grace.** Despite Jacob's unspiritual response, God was gracious enough not to take back His covenant. He was willing to be called "the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob" (Ex 3:6). (Guzik) https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-28/

## Where Protestant Traditions Differ

### Reformed (Ligonier.org)
The Reformed reading emphasises **God's sovereign, unconditional election**. God sought Jacob; Jacob was not seeking God. The contrast between Babel (man reaching up) and Bethel (God coming down) is highlighted. Calvin is quoted: Christ is the "medium" of all heavenly blessing. The promise to Jacob is seen as an "early indication" that all those with faith in the Messiah will inherit the earth (Gal 3:29; Matt 5:5). The emphasis falls on God's covenant faithfulness — "whom God loves he never leaves." (Ligonier) https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/jacobs-ladder

### Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word / David Guzik)
Guzik strongly emphasizes the **contrast between God's unconditional grace and Jacob's conditional, immature faith**. He reads Jacob's "If…" as a genuine bargain, not a pious "since." The application is intensely practical: believers must learn to trust God's word before seeing fulfilment. Guzik also makes much of the **Spurgeon quote** emphasising God's presence as the greatest blessing, and the Christological interpretation of the ladder via John 1:51. (Guzik) https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-28/

### Evangelical / Dispensational (Dr. Constable / DTS)
Constable draws on Keil & Delitzsch and Walton, noting the Hebrew *can* be read "since" rather than "if." He is more measured about Jacob's fault, describing Jacob's commitment as "somewhat selfish and conditional" rather than entirely unspiritual. He places the narrative in a detailed chiastic structure and notes parallels with ancient Near Eastern law (Nuzi tablets regarding oral blessings). Constable also traces the "I am with you" promise through Scripture as a unifying theme. (Constable) https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/genesis-28.html

### Anglican / Older (Ellicott)
Ellicott flatly states the common translation of v.21 ("then shall the Lord be my God") is **"a false translation, and gives a wrong sense."** He reads Jacob's vow as implying "no doubt on his part" but as an acceptance of covenant terms. This is a significant interpretive difference from Guzik's reading. Ellicott also provides detail on the Hebrew word *qahal* ("assembly of peoples") as foreshadowing the church. (Ellicott) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/28.htm

---

## Other Views

### Modern Scholarship
- **The "ladder" as ziggurat.** Dr. Constable notes that some interpreters (citing C. Houtman, *Vetus Testamentum* 1977) take the *sullam* as an allusion to a Mesopotamian ziggurat — a temple-tower with a monumental staircase. Others see it as the natural slope of the mountain at Bethel. (Constable) https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/genesis-28.html
- **Ligonier** similarly notes the ziggurat connection and the Babel contrast. (Ligonier) https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/jacobs-ladder
- **The *Baitylia* connection.** Ellicott notes that Phoenicians reportedly worshipped stones called *Baitylia* ("stones possessed with a soul"), possibly a corruption of Hebrew *Beth-Elohim*. However, he rejects any suggestion of idolatrous intent in Jacob's pillar — it was a memorial, not an object of worship. Later prohibitions against standing stones (Lev 26:1; Deut 16:22) addressed later corruptions of the practice. (Ellicott) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/28.htm

### Catholic and Orthodox readings
I was unable to access the Catholic/Orthodox pages (newadvent.org, catholic.com, oca.org) within the search and fetch limits. A dedicated search there would likely surface the patristic reading (e.g., St. John Chrysostom and St. Augustine both treated the ladder as a type of the Incarnation and the Cross, with Mary sometimes seen as the ladder — *Scala Jacob*). The *Catechism* references are worth noting (though I could not confirm from the sites): the ladder is traditionally seen as a prefiguration of Christ the Mediator and of the Church as the place where heaven and earth meet.

### Prosperity / Word of Faith
No material from these traditions appeared in the searches. However, Guzik's warning that Jacob's "bargaining" with God ("If You give me bread and clothing… then You will be my God") is **not** a model for prayer touches indirectly on the prosperity-gospel misreading of this text. Guzik explicitly contrasts Jacob's self-centred conditions with the God-centred nature of true faith. (Guzik) https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-28/

*Sources accessed: EnduringWord.com (David Guzik), Ellicott's Commentary (BibleHub), Dr. Constable's Expository Notes (StudyLight), Ligonier.org Reformed devotionals, Pulpit Commentary Homiletics (BibleHub), and Precept Austin devotional commentary.*
